q: `SELECT ... ORDER BY id LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000`. What does Postgres do with the first 100000 rows?
options: Reads them and throws them away
Skips them instantly with the index
Caches them for the next page
Never touches them
why: OFFSET does not jump. The deeper the page, the slower the query.

q: While a user is on page 2, new rows are added at the top of the list. They press 'next'. What can happen with OFFSET?
options: Nothing, pages are fixed
Rows can repeat, or be skipped, because the pages shift
Postgres raises an error
The next page is always empty
why: OFFSET counts rows from the top. When rows are added or deleted above you, the pages shift.

q: What does keyset pagination ask the database?
options: Skip N rows, then give me 20
Give me page number 5
Give me 20 rows after the last row I saw
Give me every row, and I will slice it
why: Keyset says after this row. The cost is the same for every page.

q: In keyset pagination you sort by `created_at`. Why add `id` as the last sort column?
options: id makes the query shorter
Postgres needs id to read the index
Without id the cursor becomes text
Many rows can share the same created_at, and the sort must be unique so no row is skipped or repeated
why: Add the primary key as the last column, in the ORDER BY and in the cursor.

q: When is OFFSET still a fine choice?
options: Small tables where you need page numbers
Infinite feeds with millions of rows
Public APIs with deep pages
Never
why: OFFSET for small tables and page numbers. Keyset for big tables, feeds and APIs.

q: How can your API know if there is a next page without a second query?
options: Run COUNT(*) on every request
Ask for size + 1 rows. If you get the extra one, there is a next page
Always return a next page link
Look at the table size in the catalog
why: The cursor is the last row, packed into text.
